turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that she could not pretend to understand his motives, but she could not feel so highly against him as he believed.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that his character had been most grossly misrepresented and that he could not expect her to credit his assertions without proof.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that she believed he was mistaken in expecting her to credit his assertions when he had not yet made them clear.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr. Darcy insisted that he had hoped to be able to convince her of the truth, but that he must now endure her disbelief.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth insisted that Mr Darcy must be aware of the grounds of his reproach, and that she could not be expected to offer them.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy insisted that he had done everything in his power to rectify his past mistakes and hoped that she would one day see him in a different light.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that his efforts to rectify his past did little to change her opinion of him and that she could not overlook the wrongs he had committed.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy insisted that his intentions had always been honourable, despite the impression he had given to Elizabeth and others, and hoped that she would eventually come to understand his true character.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that his declaration of honourable intentions was unlikely to alter her feelings towards him, given his past actions and the pain they had caused.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy told Elizabeth that he understood her feelings and acknowledged the hurt he had caused, but he could not help what he felt for her and hoped she might one day feel the same.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that his sentiments, though unexpected, had left her more convinced than ever of the necessity of their separation and that she could never view him as anything but a gentleman to be avoided.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy told Elizabeth that his feelings for her remained unchanged despite her rejection and that he hoped she might one day see him in a different light.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that she appreciated his candour but could not accept his sentiments, as his past actions had caused her and her family considerable pain.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy told Elizabeth that he regretted the pain his actions had caused but that his feelings for her were sincere and beyond his control.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that she understood his sentiments but could not disregard the past and the harm his actions had caused her and her family, and she asked him to leave her alone.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy told Elizabeth that he understood her sentiments and would respect her wishes, though it pained him to leave her in such a state of distress.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth insisted that Mr Darcy leave now and that she required time to reflect on their conversation.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy told Elizabeth that he would depart immediately and hoped for the day when she might see him in a different light, though he understood the futility of such hope at present.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth watched Mr Darcy as he left, her heart heavy with the knowledge that she could not return his feelings despite his sincere declaration.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy paused at the door, his eyes meeting Elizabeth’s one last time before he turned and walked away, his heart heavy with disappointment but resolved to respect her wishes.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that he had struggled in vain and that it would not do. His feelings would not be repressed, and he must allow him to tell her how ardently he admired and loved her.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth replied to Mr. Darcy that in such cases, it was believed to be the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It was natural that obligation should be felt, and if she could feel gratitude, she would now thank him. But she could not, for she had never desired his good opinion, and he had certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. She was sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone, but it had been most unconsciously done and she hoped it would be of short duration. The feelings which he told her had long prevented the acknowledgment of his regard could have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that this was all the reply which he was to have the honour of expecting. He might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, he was thus rejected. But it was of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that she might as well ask why, with such a clear intention of offending and insulting her, he chose to tell her that he liked her against his will, against his reason, and even against his character. Was not this some excuse for incivility, if she was uncivil? But she had other provocations. He knew she had. Had not her own feelings decided against him, had they been indifferent, or even favourable, did he think that any consideration would tempt her to accept the man who had been the means of ruining, perhaps forever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that she had every reason in the world to think ill of him. No motive could excuse the unjust and ungenerous part he had acted there. He dared not, he could not deny that he had been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that it was not merely this affair on which her dislike was founded. Long before it had taken place, her opinion of him was decided. His character was unfolded in the recital which she had received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what could he have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship could he here defend himself? Or under what misrepresentation could he here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that she took an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth replied to Mr. Darcy that who that knew what his misfortunes had been could help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that his misfortunes had indeed been great indeed.
